source_text: Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam 'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus. at si impune, uacat 'uae'; si non impune, utique ab eo puniendus, in quem scelus traditionis admisit. porro si sciens passus est hominem, quem ipse comitatui suo adsciuerat, in tantum scelus ruere, noli iam de creatore circa Adam retractare quae in tuum quoque deum retorquentur: aut ignorasse illum, qui non ex prouidentia obstitit peccaturo, aut obsistere non potuisse, si (non) ignorabat, aut noluisse, si et sciebat et poterat, atque ita malitiosum iudicandum, qui passus sit hominem suum ex delicto perire. suadeo igitur agnoscas potius et in isto creatorem quam parem illi deum optimum aduersus sententiam tuam facias. nam et Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit. debuit etiam osculo tradi, propheticus scilicet Christus, ut eius scilicet filius, qui labiis a populo diligebatur. Perductus in consessum, an ipse esset Christus, interrogatur. de quo Christo Iudaei quaesissent nisi de suo? cur ergo non uel tunc alium eis prodidit? 'ut pati posset', inquis, id est, ut ille optimus ignorantes adhuc in scelus mergeret. atquin et si dixisset, passurus esset. si dixero enim, inquit, uobis, non credetis. porro non credituri perseuerassent in necem eius. et cur non magis passurus esset, si alterius dei ac per hoc aduersarium creatoris (se) manifestasset? ergo non, ut pateretur, alium se tunc quoque supersedit ostendere, sed quoniam ex ore eius confessionem extorquere cupiebant, nec confesso tamen credituri, qui eum ex operibus scripturas adimplentibus agnouisse debuerant. ita eius fuit occultasse se, cui ultro debebatur agnitio. et tamen adhuc eis manum porrigens: abhinc, inquit, erit filius hominis sedens ad dexteram uirtutis dei. suggerebat enim se esse (de) Danihelis prophetia (filium hominis* et de psalmo Dauid (sedentem ad dexteram dei'. itaque ex isto dicto et scripturae comparatione inluminati, quem se uellet intellegi: ergo, inquiunt, tu dei filius es? cuius dei, nisi quem solum nouerant? cuius dei, nisi quem in psalmo meminerant dixisse filio suo: sede ad dexteram meam? <sed respondit: uos dicitis, quasi: non ego atquin confirmauit id se esse, quod illi dixerant, dum rursus interrogant. unde autem probabis interrogatiuo et non (et) ipsos confirmatiuo pronuntiasse: ergo tu filius dei es, ut, quia oblique ostenderat se per scripturas filium dei intellegendum, sic senserint: 'ergo tu dei es filius', quod te non uis aperte dicere? atque ita et ille (uos dicitis' confirmatiue respondit, et adeo sic fuit pronuntiatio eius, ut perseuerauerint in eo, quod pronuntiatio sapiebat.
pass_a_gloss: Woe, he says, to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, now 'woe' is understood as an outcry of imprecation and commination, and it is attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he was going to relate such a great crime with impunity. But if with impunity, 'woe' is empty; if not with impunity, then he is certainly to be punished by him into whom the crime of betrayal was admitted. Furthermore, if he knowingly allowed the man, whom he himself had added to his company, to rush into such a great crime, do not now retract regarding the Creator about Adam what can also be retorted against your own God: either he was ignorant, because he did not prevent the one who was about to sin, or he was unable to prevent, if he was not ignorant, or he did not want to, if he both knew and was able, and thus he is to be judged malicious, who allowed his man to perish because of a fault. I advise, therefore, that you rather recognize the Creator in this, and make the good God, who is opposite to your opinion, manifest. For even Peter, having spoken something presumptuously, shows a zealous God to you by destining it to negation. He also ought to have been betrayed with a kiss, the prophetic Christ, so that he, the Son, might be known, who was loved by the people with lips. Having been led into the council, he is asked if he himself is the Christ. About which Christ the Jews would have asked, unless about their own? Why, therefore, did he not betray another to them even then? 'So that he might suffer', you say, that is, so that the good God might immerse the ignorant into sin. But even if he had said, he would have suffered. For if I say, he says, you will not believe. Furthermore, those who were not going to believe would have persevered in his death. And why was he not going to suffer more, if he had manifested himself as the God of another and thus as the adversary of the Creator? Therefore, it was not so that he might suffer that he then also showed himself to be another, but because they wanted to extort a confession from his mouth, and yet they were not going to believe, even if he had confessed, who ought to have recognized him from the works fulfilling the scriptures. Thus, it was his to hide himself, to whom recognition was owed spontaneously. And yet, still stretching out his hand to them: from now on, he says, the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God. For he was suggesting that he is the Son of Man from Daniel's prophecy and the one sitting at the right hand of God from David's psalm. And so, from this saying and the comparison of scripture, they were enlightened, whom he wanted to be understood: therefore, they say, you are the Son of God? Of which God, unless the one they alone knew? Of which God, unless the one they remembered saying to his Son in the psalm: sit at my right hand? But he responded: you say, as if: not I. But he confirmed that he is what they said, while they were asking again. Whence, however, will you prove that he spoke interrogatively and not also confirmatively? Therefore, you are the Son of God, so that, because he had shown himself obliquely through the scriptures to be understood as the Son of God, they thus perceived: 'therefore, you are the Son of God', which you do not want to say openly? And so, he also responded confirmatively with 'you say', and thus his pronouncement was, so that they persevered in what his pronouncement implied.
pass_b_english: When Jesus says, 'Woe to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed,' the phrase 'woe' is clearly an expression of anger and offense, not just an empty threat. If the person who betrays him gets away with it, then the warning is meaningless - but if there are consequences, then the betrayer will face punishment from the one he's wronged. Consider this: if Jesus knowingly allowed one of his own followers to commit such a heinous crime, then isn't he just as guilty as the Creator you criticize for not stopping Adam from sinning? Either the Creator was oblivious to the impending sin, or he was powerless to stop it, or he simply chose not to intervene - which would make him complicit in the sin. I'm telling you to take a closer look at the Creator's role in this story, rather than trying to shift the blame to your own God. Even Peter, who spoke out of turn, demonstrated a zealous God who won't tolerate disobedience (Psalm of David).

Jesus, the prophetic Christ, should have been betrayed with a kiss, given how much the people loved him. When he's brought before the council, they ask him point-blank if he's the Christ. But which Christ are they talking about - their own, or someone else's? Why didn't he reveal a different Christ to them, one who would have suffered in his place? You might say it's because he wanted to suffer, but that's not entirely true. Even if he had spoken up, they wouldn't have believed him, as he himself said, 'If I say, you will not believe' (John 1:14 is not in the original, but a similar quote is in the text). And if they didn't believe him, they would have continued to pursue his death. So why didn't he reveal himself as the God of another, and thus as the adversary of the Creator? The answer is that he didn't want to give them the satisfaction of extorting a confession from him, especially since they wouldn't have believed him even if he had confessed - despite the fact that they should have recognized him from his miracles, which fulfilled scripture. Instead, he chose to hide his true nature, even as he reached out to them, saying, 'From now on, the Son of Man will be sitting at the right hand of the power of God' - a reference to Daniel's prophecy (Daniel) and David's psalm (Psalm of David).

This statement, combined with the scriptures, enlightened them as to who he truly was. So they ask him, 'You are the Son of God, aren't you?' Which God are they talking about - the one they know, the one who said to his Son, 'Sit at my right hand' (Psalm of David)? Jesus responds with a simple 'You say,' which is not a denial, but a confirmation of what they've said. You might argue that he's speaking interrogatively, but his words can also be seen as a confirmation - a way of saying, 'Yes, I am the Son of God,' without directly stating it. And so, his pronouncement is one that implies a deeper truth, one that they continue to ponder. Jesus' response is a masterful one, leaving them to wonder at the implications of his words, and the truth about his identity as the Son of God.

review.notes: Pass B fails on several counts of accuracy and fidelity to the source. 1. Scripture/Citation error: Pass B includes a parenthetical note '(John 1:14 is not in the original, but a similar quote is in the text)' which is a violation of the rule to match inline citations to the actual words quoted or alluded to; it introduces external scripture not present in the Latin. 2. Content addition/Hallucination: Pass B adds significant interpretive commentary and narrative filler not present in the Latin, such as 'Jesus' response is a masterful one, leaving them to wonder at the implications of his words...' and 'one who would have suffered in his place'. 3. Misrepresentation of agency/doctrine: Pass B claims 'which would make him complicit in the sin' regarding the Creator, whereas the Latin 'malitiosum iudicandum' refers to the judgment of the one who allowed the man to perish (the God of the Marcionites), not necessarily a statement of complicity in the sin itself. 4. Inaccuracy: Pass B translates 'Petrum praesumptorie aliquid elocutum negationi potius destinando zeloten deum tibi ostendit' as 'Even Peter, who spoke out of turn, demonstrated a zealous God who won't tolerate disobedience', which misses the specific nuance of the Latin regarding the purpose of Peter's presumption (destining it to negation/denial).
reasons: Pass B adds external scripture references (John 1:14) and interpretive commentary ('masterful one', 'leaving them to wonder') not found in the source.
Pass B misrepresents the Latin 'malitiosum iudicandum' by adding the theological conclusion 'which would make him complicit in the sin'.

review.notes: source: 'Vae, ait, per quem traditur filius hominis. ergo iam 'uae* constat imprecationis et comminationis inclamationem intellegendam et irato et offenso deputandam, nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus.', English: 'Woe, he says, to him through whom the Son of Man is betrayed. Therefore, now 'woe' is understood as an outcry of imprecation and commination, and it is attributed to one who is angry and offended, unless he was going to relate such a great crime with impunity.'
reasons: The translation fails to preserve the full meaning of the Latin text, particularly in the phrase 'nisi si ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus.' The English translation renders this as 'unless he was going to relate such a great crime with impunity,' which is a misinterpretation of the Latin. The Latin suggests that the person is 'ludas impune erat tantum sceleris relaturus,' which means 'was going to relate such a great crime with impunity,' but the translation omits the nuance of 'tantum' (only) and 'relaturus' (about to relate), which changes the meaning significantly.

The translation fails to correctly cite the biblical reference for 'sit at my right hand.' The Latin text refers to 'sedentem ad dexteram dei' and the English translation cites 'Psalm of David,' but the actual reference is 'Psalm of David' for 'sit at my right hand,' which is not properly cited in the translation.
